title: Rabies elimination
author: none@none.com (Muhammad Aftab Gohar)
content:
IT begins with a fever, a headache and a restlessness that will not settle. Then the patient panics at the sight of water. After days of going from hospital to hospital, the family learns that a dog bite weeks or months earlier, long healed and forgotten, carried rabies. The virus has reached the brain, and there is no cure.
This scene plays out in hospitals across Pakistan every week, yet every such death is preventable. Sindh, where reporting has improved, recorded 285,000 dog bites in 2025 and over 200,000 by September 2026, with at least 41 rabies deaths this year. The Indus Hospital also saw rabies cases from Balochistan, and eight more came through teleconsultation from across the country. Punjab reported more than 1.3 million dog-bite cases between 2021 and March 2026. Estimates put Pakistan’s rabies deaths at 2,000 to 5,000 a year, most of them poor and many of them children.
A study published this year in eBioMedicine, a Lancet journal, which I co-authored with Indus Hospital and Erasmus MC colleagues, shows how widely the virus circulates. We found rabies virus in 64 of 100 severe dog-bite wounds in Karachi, and two-thirds of the patients were children. It covered only severe bites, so it does not mean two in three biting dogs are rabid, but the warning is stark. If this is the picture in a city with the province’s best-equipped bite clinics, it is unlikely to be better elsewhere in Sindh or Pakistan.
Elimination needs action on five fronts. The first is surveillance. Behind every reported case is a grieving family. Much of the recent rise reflects improved surveillance, and the true burden is still hidden. Many families believe the patient is possessed and turn to a shrine, not a hospital; others die in hospital undiagnosed. Surveillance must keep improving, with human rabies and dog bites notifiable at every level, so that reliable data reveals the true burden and where to focus resources. Swabbing bite wounds can also track the virus without catching dogs.
Vaccine and immunoglobulin must be free at every public facility.
The second is awareness. Children, especially boys, often tease street dogs and cannot defend themselves when attacked; peaceful coexistence starts with how we treat community dogs. Every household should know to wash a bite wound with soap and running water for 15 minutes, then seek immediate treatment at an anti-rabies centre, since washing reduces the virus but does not remove it. These messages belong in school curricula, mosques and the media.
The third is correct treatment. Rabies is almost 100 per cent preventable with timely post-exposure prophylaxis, and in our study nearly 96pc of patients developed protective antibodies. Yet roughly half of the rabies deaths reported at our centres occur in people whose treatment was incomplete or wrongly given. Immunoglobulin remains scarce, and too many patients drop out before finishing the course. Vaccine and immunoglobulin must be free at every public facility, and every doctor and nurse treating bites must be trained to WHO guidelines. The Sindh government’s ongoing rabies campaign deserves credit and, if sustained, can save many lives.
The fourth is mass dog vaccination, because treating people alone will never end rabies. When at least 70pc of dogs are vaccinated year after year, the virus stops circulating. In September 2026, WHO validated Bhutan as the first country in WHO’s South-East Asia Region to eliminate dog-transmitted human rabies.
The fifth is effective dog population management. Uncollected garbage feeds street dogs, which is why katchi abadis have the most dogs and the most bites. Views differ on the best methods, but any approach must be hu­­mane, gu­­i­ded by evidence and international standards, sustained over time, and backed by proper waste management and responsible ownership. Local governments, veterinary services and communities must agree on what works locally and monitor results.
None of this can succeed in isolation. Health, livestock, local government and education departments each hold a piece and must work together under the One Health approach. The federal health minister’s in-principle approval of a National Rabies Prevention and Control Framework in July 2026 offers real hope. With timely notification, sustained funding and clear, measurable targets, it could become the turning point Pakistan has long awaited, with the media and civil society holding every institution to account.
The global goal is zero deaths from dog-transmitted rabies by 2030. Bhutan has shown it can be done. A rabies-free Pakistan is within reach if we act together, and act now.
The writer is technical lead, Rabies Prevention, Management & Training Services at the Indus Hospital & Health Network, Pakistan, and part of the National & Provincial Technical Working Advisory Group on Rabies.

summary: Rabies remains a significant, preventable public health crisis in Pakistan, causing thousands of deaths annually, predominantly among the poor and children, despite readily available preventive measures.
Current challenges include under-reporting due to poor surveillance, public unawareness, incomplete or incorrect post-exposure prophylaxis, and the scarcity of crucial treatments like immunoglobulin.

Effective elimination requires a five-pronged strategy: enhanced surveillance, widespread public awareness, free and WHO-compliant human treatment, mass dog vaccination (targeting 70% coverage), and humane, evidence-based dog population management.

A holistic "One Health" approach, involving inter-departmental collaboration (health, livestock, local government, education) and a National Rabies Prevention and Control Framework, is crucial for achieving the 2030 global elimination goal.
facts: Sindh recorded 285,000 dog bites in 2025 and over 200,000 by September 2026, with at least 41 rabies deaths in 2026.
Estimates put Pakistan’s rabies deaths at 2,000 to 5,000 a year, with most being poor and many children.
A study co-authored by the writer found rabies virus in 64 of 100 severe dog-bite wounds in Karachi, with two-thirds of the patients being children.
academicReferences: WHO Guidelines for Rabies Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (for correct treatment protocols).
One Health Approach (a global strategy for addressing interconnected health threats).
Global Goal of Zero deaths from dog-transmitted rabies by 2030 (target set by WHO, OIE, FAO, and GARC).

title: Peace prognosis
author: none@none.com (Dr Raashid Wali Janjua)
content:
AFGHAN foreign and domestic policies are a curious mix of tribalism, revanchism and ideological confusion that shun human rights and statecraft in favour of support for terrorist groups based on Afghan soil that pose a clear danger to regional peace. Unfortunately, all attempts at positive engagement with the Afghan Taliban by Pakistan as well as regional countries have been scuttled due to Kabul’s lack of willingness to rein in terrorist outfits operating under its benign gaze.
A belief has gained traction amongst the Afghan Taliban that their successful armed struggle against Nato/USA could also be emulated by their ideological comrades like Al Qaeda, IS-K, ETIM, the TTP etc in pursuit of their political objectives. Rooted in medieval notions of tribal honour and revenge, the regime offers a propitious environment for growth of terror networks. The flow of external funds into the Afghan regime’s coffers has encouraged the obduracy of the Taliban, which continues channelling these funds to its ideological allies, sustaining the vicious cycle of terrorism and crime.
    
Afghanistan is acting as a generous host for terrorist outfits that use its soil to generate economic rents through narco-trafficking, ransom, and smuggling. These groups are confident that their base of operation and sources of income would remain protected under the Taliban. A mere look at the figures showing the funding of this terror haven by the unsuspecting international community indicates why Taliban-ruled Afghanistan remains a threat.
Since August 2021, donors have confirmed paying $8 billion in humanitarian assistance to Afghanistan through various international organisations, with a further $3.78bn committed and $94 million pled­ged. Billions more were reportedly received by the Taliban regime in direct foreign grants. Western capitals remain the biggest financial contributors to Afghanistan.
The Afghan economy is kept afloat by foreign patronage and narco-trafficking.
Afghanistan imports goods worth around $12bn annually against exports of only $1.7bn, leaving an annual trade deficit of $10.3bn. It is intriguing how the Taliban regime is bridging $10.3bn every year. The answer lies in $17.5bn in foreign grants received since 2021, besides billions of dollars earned through narco-trafficking. It is clear evidence of an economy kept afloat by foreign patronage and narco-trafficking.
But the biggest question is: should such a regime that hosts terrorist groups be kept afloat through the largesse of international donors who might soon feel the heat from violent groups based in Afghanistan? If the international community thinks it can wean the Afghan Taliban away from terrorists, it needs to have a look at Pakistan’s 17 sincere attempts through ministers, the national security advisor, special representative, and joint coordination committee interactions, besides internationally mediated parleys in Doha, Istanbul, Riyadh and Urumqi.
The reason for Afghan obstinacy is hubris and ideological narcissism that are pampered through foreign indulgence, despite zero concessions by the Kandahar-based ruling clique on political inclusivity, women’s education and minority rights. Pakistan has tried bilateral channels and has exhausted relevant regional fora like the trilateral group (Pakistan, China and Afghanistan) where in 2023 the Afghan foreign minister agreed to stop the flow of terrorism from Afghan soil.
The Moscow Format, which evolved out of a quadrilateral forum which was abandoned by the US after the Ukraine War, kept pressing the Afghan regime to abide by international counterterrorism obligations till its seventh meeting. However, it failed to elicit a positive response from the Taliban delegation during its eighth iteration at Mos­cow on Oct 5.
    
The Taliban’s reluctance to even acknowledge the need to stop the ac­­tivities of terrorist groups from Afghan soil betrays a mindset that is sympathetic to these violent groups. This should be a clear message to countries like Russia that are giving space to the Taliban regime in pursuit of narrow security goals.
The fact is that all development and connectivity goals like TAPI, Casa-1000, and Trans-Afghan Railway, as well as mines and mineral exploration in Afghanistan, would remain a pipe dream till the time the Afghan Taliban stop sponsoring terrorism.
The proceeds from illegal mining go to support the Taliban’s military infrastructure. Moreover, since 2021, it has established thousands of madressahs against 269 modern schools, replaced 90,000 teachers with around 100,000 Taliban-aligned clerics, abolished 18 university disciplines, rewritten 200-plus subjects and banned 679 textbooks.
Until the Taliban regime gives up its support for terrorism and provides verifiable guarantees to Pakistan, meaningful normalisation, regional connectivity and lasting stability will not materialise.
The writer is a PhD from NUST.

title: Water crisis
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
PUNJAB’S looming water crisis should serve as a wake-up call for both federal and provincial policymakers. A new assessment by the UN Food and Agriculture Organisation warns that water demand in the province already exceeds supply across all sectors. Even more alarming is the annual depletion of 5.5bn cubic metres of groundwater. The province needs an additional 10bn cubic metres of usable water every year to bridge the supply-demand gap and sustain its aquifer. This shows the consequences of years of neglect and an approach to water management that has placed little emphasis on conservation. The FAO findings are based on water accounts covering 2012-17 but the trends hold. Punjab’s agricultural economy, expanding cities and growing population are placing increasing pressure on a resource that is already under severe stress.
Agriculture, which accounts for the bulk of freshwater use, must be central to any serious conservation strategy. Much of Punjab still relies on traditional flood irrigation, an inefficient method that results in substantial losses. There is an urgent need to encourage a transition towards water-efficient technologies. This can help farmers produce more with less water. Crop choices also need to reflect local water availability. Furthermore, there is a case for developing smaller, distributed water storage facilities along riverbeds and suitable locations in the riverine belt. Such reservoirs, including off-channel storage and recharge ponds where feasible, could capture surplus flows during periods of high availability for use when supplies fall. This would offer a complementary and potentially cheaper option to large dams, whose construction involves substantial financial, environmental and social costs. Much of the rain that cities receive is channelled into drainage and sewerage systems due to rapid construction and the spread of concrete. Better urban planning must make rainwater harvesting, permeable surfaces, recharge wells and retention ponds integral to new housing schemes and public infrastructure. Cities need investment in systems that capture and store rainwater. Wastewater treatment and reuse, too, should become part of the province’s water strategy. The FAO’s proposal for a provincial water commission similarly deserves serious consideration.

title: Being civil to begin with
author: none@none.com (Jawed Naqvi)
content:
THAT Pakistan is sending a minister to attend the SCO Civilisational Dialogue in New Delhi on Nov 20 should be applauded even if it’s not clear that this could be the proverbial ice breaker between the perpetually aloof neighbours. It is, however, worth hoping for.
The agenda for a civilisational dialogue should be fun for the participants, although India’s decade-old Hindu revivalist government may drag its feet on the issue. Bilateral ties can still improve despite this handicap. Reports are circulating of cross-border trade also picking up — albeit discreetly — between India and Pakistan in recent days.
Renowned political analyst Trita Parsi used a phrase to describe the options for a low-key US retreat from the war-torn Gulf region, which may be relevant for India-Pakistan ties. Parsi likened Donald Trump’s options for a face-saving pullout from his self-created mess to Swiss cheese. Sanctions on paper and holes inside, like the bubbles within a good Swiss cheese. The US could keep its formal sanctions on the books so the administration can publicly claim it is still maintaining pressure on Tehran. In reality, the enforcement is invisibly relaxed. Which is what might work, if nothing else does, for the South Asian neighbours — an unannounced, even surreptitious discarding of different stages of hostilities.
Behind the scenes, in Parsi’s version of a workable Gulf resolution, the US gradually loosens its naval blockade and stops aggressively enforcing sanctions. This creates large “holes” in the economic pressure — much like the Swiss cheese — allowing Asian, Middle Eastern, and Gulf countries to resume trading with and investing in Iran without fear of US retaliation. At some opportune moment, even if the currently tense atmosphere results in another catastrophic flare-up, peace would be the only game in town, possibly giving credence to Trita Parsi’s face-saving device.
    
The immediate trigger for the latest round of signalling, if it indeed adds up to some kind of undeclared rapprochement, springs from very practical and commonsensical exigencies that require all neighbours to collectively deal with the huge economic challenges dogging the world. The platform offered by the SCO has been used and abused by both sides in the past to launch verbal attacks on each other. Could the tide have turned?
The agenda at hand for Dr Musadik Malik, Federal Minister for Climate Change and Environmental Coordination, representing Pak­is­tan at the meeting could present challenges as well as chances to resolve them. However, the lar­ger theme of a civilisational dialogue that brings all SCO members together may have to confront some predictable handwringing from India.
An unannounced, even surreptitious discarding of different stages of hostilities could work for South Asia.
The idea of civilisation imagines a palpable and unbroken link between the past and the present. In its understanding of India’s past, however, the Hindutva establishment in New Delhi has manufactured demons to comply with a narrow political agenda. Its search for a golden past requires changing names of streets, and identifying, abusing and occasionally lynching the conjured enemy.
Pakistan has been through this motion in the past. That’s when schoolchildren were given controversial ideas about non-Muslims. An instructive moment came when a Muslim journalist from India who accompanied Atal Bihari Vajpayee on his visit to Pakistan in 1978 went with his colleagues to meet his cousins. At the emotional meeting, they also wanted to know discreetly if K.K. Katyal, Raghu Rai and Sumit Chakravarty were Hindu. “But they are just like us,” one cousin reportedly observed after being told of their Hindu identities.
Today many centres in Pakistan are exploring and retrieving old names of their neighbourhoods with a view to restoring their Hindu or other non-Muslim identity. India, with the advent of Narendra Modi, is heading in the opposite direction. Mughal rule is being airbrushed from school curriculum.
If more Indians could travel to Pakistan they would be able to see things similar to what I saw. A few days before the Lahore summit, I travelled with Sushma Swaraj and K.R. Malkani to the fabled Katas Raj Temple abutting the Lahore-Islamabad motorway. Malkani, an atheist, stood there looking amused as Swaraj dipped her hands into the sacred pond thought to have been used by the Pandavas during their exile. The caring way this temple and countless others have been preserved for Indian tourists will make more sense when people travel across the borders.
This is not to say that minorities don’t face prejudice in Pakistan. Pakistani human rights activists have spoken strongly against forcible marriage of Hindu girls. The government has made some laws to deter the phenomenon but its impact is not uniformly felt.
    
The prevalent bigotry on the Indian side finds state support often enough as it assumes the form of homes, mosques and churches being vandalised or bulldozed accompanied by the occasional lynching of individuals from minorities. There seems to be a competition between bigots from both sides.
At the SCO dialogue, a two-day session will centre on civilisational and cultural expression, art and architecture, language and literature, and religious and philosophical traditions. Delegates will also deliberate on filing joint multinational nominations for Unesco World Heritage recognition based on centuries of shared cultural exchange. Much of this will be problematic for the current ruling dispensation in India.
In 2015, it had dubiously rejected a Unesco plan to declare Delhi a World Heritage City encompassing Old Delhi with its Mughal-era icons and British-era Lutyens’ New Delhi.
To conclude, a telling story from the Maldives where Muslim zealots set fire to a Pakistani pavilion during a 2011 Saarc event and India watched the mayhem without a word of camaraderie with Pakistan. The event involved a display of national cultural treasures by Saarc states. Pakistan showcased its Buddhist heritage with tableaux of relics from Moenjodaro’s Indus civilisation. Extremists set fire to the Pakistan pavilion. The SCO dialogue offers as good an occasion as any to make amends to this witless aloofness between the two.
The writer is Dawn’s correspondent in Delhi.

title: Taxpayers’ burden
author: none@none.com (Mohammad Younus Dagha)
content:
IN challenging times, ordinary citizens and businesses may be called upon to shoulder higher tax burdens to meet the unavoidable costs of maintaining a sovereign state. But citizens should not be expected to bear the burden of costs that are largely avoidable.
When debt servicing consumes 125 per cent of the FBR taxes retained by the federal government, 68.5pc of its total revenues, and nearly three times the defence budget, such an extraordinary burden demands closer scrutiny. Is our public debt being managed prudently and efficiently?
In Pakistan, where a large proportion of the population comprises practising Muslims, many people prefer to keep their savings in bank accounts that pay no interest. As a result, nearly 40pc of all bank deposits are held in current accounts, on which banks pay no interest. This gives Pakistani banks access to an exceptionally cheap source of funds, which they invest in government securities at exorbitantly high returns.
According to the State Bank of Pakistan, banks paid an average interest rate of just 5.53pc on their total deposits in September 2026, including current accounts that pay no interest. Yet, in October 2026, the government was borrowing through 12-month treasury bills at 12.79pc — a gross difference of 7.26 percentage points.
Is our public debt being managed prudently and efficiently?
A prudent borrower would certainly have sought to negotiate a much narrower margin, perhaps 1-2 percentage points. Yet our government continues to borrow at substantially higher rates, raising serious questions about the management of public debt. Ultimately, taxpayers are asked to bear the cost of such generosity. The burden falls on petrol and diesel consumers paying the Petroleum Development Levy, as well as investors paying effective income tax rates of 50-60pc.
High returns on relatively low-risk government securities have encouraged banks to attract more low-cost deposits, particularly current accounts. By June 2026, these accounts held Rs15.3 trillion, nearly 40pc of total deposits, up from 37pc a year earlier. SBP confirms that the Rs3.67tn increase in deposits during the first half of 2026 came mainly from current accounts.
While much of Pakistan’s productive economy has struggled, bank deposits have tripled from Rs13.35tn in December 2018 to nearly Rs41tn in September 2026. But where has this enormous pool of savings gone? Into new industries, businesses and jobs, or increasingly into high-yield government securities, earning banks substantial returns at taxpayers’ expense?
According to SBP, commercial banks held Rs40.36tn in government securities in September 2026. Applying the prevailing gross interest-rate differential of 7.26 percentage points to these holdings gives an estimated annualised differential of approximately Rs2.93tn.
If government borrowing rates were limited to 1-2 percentage points above banks’ average deposit cost, the estimated annualised gross savings could reach Rs2,100-2,500 billion, subject to debt maturities and repricing. Even part of these savings could ease the lives of millions of households and thousands of struggling entrepreneurs by reducing the Petroleum Development Levy, multiple taxes on energy bills, and high income tax rates on salaries and businesses.
Such a policy would also reduce SBP’s annual interest earnings by approximately Rs118bn, which would be just a fraction of the overall savings.
What needs to be done?
The government should introduce a law that limits the interest paid to commercial banks on government securities to a reasonable 1-2 percentage points above what banks pay their depositors on average. The implementation process should ensure that monetary policy, government borrowing operations and financial stability are not disrupted.
In order to bring transparency into debt management operations, the law should require the Ministry of Finance and SBP to publish quarterly reports showing how much the government borrows from banks and other investors, the interest it pays, and the cost of funds to banks. These reports should also disclose how much the government actually saves through lower borrowing costs.
The potential annual savings of Rs2,100-2,500bn, once realised, should be passed on to taxpayers and businesses that have long borne the burden of excessive taxation, rather than being absorbed by increased government expenditure. The priority should be to reduce the Petroleum Development Levy and General Sales Tax on electricity bills, thereby lowering fuel and transport costs, easing the cost of living and production, and reducing inflationary pressures. The government should also double the annual income-tax exemption threshold from Rs600,000 to Rs1.2 million, providing much-needed relief to salaried individuals and low-income taxpayers.
The government should also restore the Final Tax Regime for exporters, making tax deducted from export proceeds their final income tax liability, even if the rate remains 2pc. This would simplify taxation, eliminate uncertainty and improve the competitiveness of Pakistani exporters by bringing their tax treatment closer to that of competitors in peer economies.
Equally important is the complete abolition of the super tax, which reportedly generates around Rs400-500bn annually, but has become a major deterrent to new investment. The highest effective income tax rate on corporate, business and other incomes should be capped at 35pc, making Pakistan more attractive to investors while leaving greater disposable income available for savings, consumption and investment.
Many such measures could be financed through the proposed annual debt-servicing savings of Rs2,100-2,500bn, provided the government pursues the necessary reforms with determination and ensures that the resulting fiscal space is used to reduce the tax burden rather than expand public expenditure. These measures would provide a much-needed stimulus to economic growth, encourage investment and job creation, and help alleviate poverty, which has become one of the country’s most pressing challenges.
Reviving economic growth requires reducing the excessive tax burden on ordinary citizens and businesses — a burden that stifles investment, discourages enterprise and holds back economic activity.
The writer is former federal finance secretary and currently chairman, Policy Research and Advisory Council.

title: The IWT dilemma
author: none@none.com (Aisha Khan)
content:
THE Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) of 1960 has long been heralded as one of the most durable water-sharing agreements in history. Despite multiple wars and decades of profound political animosity between India and Pakistan, the IWT managed to survive, providing a fragile framework for regulating the shared waters of the Indus River system.
However, the delicate equilibrium of this treaty has been shattered. The move by India to place the IWT in abeyance is not merely a diplomatic protest; it represents a fundamental strategic pivot.
In an era increasingly defined by climate change and existential resource competition, the suspension of the IWT signals a shift toward a new, perilous world order where water security dictates state survival, and historical norms are rapidly eclipsed by the “law of the jungle.”
To understand the severity of the hydro-political reality of scarcity, one must look beyond the immediate geopolitical friction and consider the changing hydrology and demography of the region. Climate change is rapidly altering the cryosphere of the Himalayas, which feeds the Indus basin. Glacial retreat, erratic monsoon patterns, and severe, prolonged droughts are making water availability increasingly unpredictable.
    
The World Resources Institute (WRI) provides a stark warning in its Aqueduct Water Risk Atlas, mapping a future where water becomes the most prized — and contentious — resource on the planet. According to WRI projections, vast swathes of the globe, including South Asia, face escalating levels of baseline water stress. By mid-century, trillions of dollars in GDP will be exposed to high water risk as demand drastically outstrips renewable supply. In such a landscape, water is no longer just an environmental issue; it is a fundamental driver of national security.
As resources diminish, states are becoming increasingly inward-looking. The international order, which once placed a premium on cooperation, is giving way to a more ruthless framework where states prioritise their own existential needs above collective agreements.
In this light, placing the IWT in abeyance is not a temporary diplomatic manoeuvre; it is a strategic preparation of the ground for an eventual unilateral withdrawal.
As water scarcity increases, the temptation for an upper-riparian state to leverage control over water flows to secure its own agricultural and energy requirements becomes overwhelming, effectively treating the resource as sovereign property rather than a shared heritage.
For Pakistan, the stakes are high because the Indus basin underpins agricultural production, rural livelihoods and food security.
The intensification of India’s construction of storage dams along the Chenab River, despite the legal challenges and protests from Pakistan, is part of the strategic calculus and entirely consistent with this new paradigm. These projects allow for greater control, storage, and diversion of water.
For Pakistan, an agrarian economy whose very existence relies on the Indus system, this is not a developmental disagreement — it is an existential threat. The Chenab-Beas link tunnel and the Salal sediment bypass illustrate the dilemma.
Such projects may be presented as engineering responses to energy needs and sedimentation, yet transferring water between basins or modifying sediment-control infrastructure on a shared river raises both questions and concerns. The legal status and technical details of each project must be assessed individually for cumulative impact and downstream confidence.
In August 2026 the Court of Arbitration rejected India’s unilateral abeyance of the treaty and reaffirmed that it remains in force. The court also ordered interim measures restricting specified construction at the Ratle hydroelectric project till 90 days after the Neutral Expert’s final decision expected in July 2027. India’s rejection of the court’s authority leaves a gap between legal pronouncement and practical compliance.
The coming decision on pondage, spillways, low-level outlets and sediment flushing will matter, but the deeper question is whether both will accept a credible process for resolving disagreements. If the Neutral Expert and Court of Arbitration reach conflicting conclusions, and one or both governments dismiss the outcome, the treaty risks becoming an instrument that exists formally but no longer commands confidence.
An institutional collapse would have consequences extending far beyond the immediate available water. It could erode hydrological data sharing, weaken flood warning cooperation, discourage investment in regional water management and intensify competition over reservoirs and infrastructure.
A breakdown could also encourage unilateralism in transboundary river governance endangering peace at a time of growing geopolitical tensions and environmental fragility. The central danger remains the growing uncertainty in a system already under intense human pressure.
    
For Pakistan, the stakes are high because the Indus basin underpins agricultural production, rural livelihoods and food security. For India, the consequences would include a more volatile neighbourhood, heightened diplomatic costs and a precedent that could complicate its own relations with other upstream countries. Neither country can insulate itself from the climatic and economic consequences of a destabilised basin.
The gravity of the situation is exacerbated by the nuclear capabilities of both nations. The failure of the current global negotiations in limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius is also ensuring that hydrological instability will only worsen and add to the fear of scarcity.
The international community must act before the legal impasse becomes a humanitarian and security crisis. Political wisdom and environmental diplomacy can also play a major role in averting a potential catastrophe.
A nuclear-armed upstream power and a highly water-dependent nuclear-armed lower-riparian state cannot afford to let a river become an instrument of existential threat. If water insecurity contributes to political instability, military escalation or a wider regional confrontation, the consequences will not remain confined to South Asia.
The writer is a climate policy analyst.

title: Symbol of neglect
author: none@none.com (Arooj Waheed Dar)
content:
NOTHING quite prepares you for the sensory overload you experience when you move from the pristine and polished Islamabad to the battered and potholed Karachi.
To the discerning eye, Karachi looks like a low-resolution version of Islamabad, that too in sepia tones. The vibrancy of the “City of Lights” is mellowed by the haze of suspended smoke and dust, further muted by the drabness of its infrastructure. Its skyline, characterised by decrepit buildings woven through a not-so-intricate web of overhead wires, pales in comparison with Islamabad’s lush green, hilly landscape.
The sounds of each city also stand in sharp contrast. While the latest and most luxurious private cars noiselessly cruise through Islamabad’s roads, Karachi’s streets are swarmed with motorbikes, rickshaws, buses, and trucks, each incessantly blaring its horn to force its way through traffic. Many private vehicles on the road bear visible signs of abuse inflicted by other heedless drivers.
Both cities have their distinct olfactory signatures as well: while Islamabad exudes privilege and dewy freshness, Karachi reeks of injustice, neglect, and just pure garbage. The stench emanating from gutters, garbage sites, and at times, the sea is so overpowering that even the confines of an air-conditioned car fail to offer any respite from the pungency.
Karachi’s disparity is unfortunate given its economic footprint.
On the development front, as Islamabad witnesses the construction of new underpasses and bridges on a near-monthly basis, Karachi’s infrastructure crumbles under the weight of its burgeoning population, exacerbated by the governance conundrum it faces. The city remains in shambles, ranking 170th out of 173 cities on the EIU’s Global Liveability Index 2026.
This disparity is particularly unfortunate given Karachi’s enormous economic footprint, not to mention its remarkable capacity to embrace people from diverse backgrounds. The city accounts for nearly a quarter of Pakistan’s GDP, compared to Islamabad’s estimated 1-2 per cent. Yet, despite being nearly four times larger in area and having more than 10 times Islamabad’s population, Karachi receives a smaller share of development allocations. Whatever resources are earmarked for the city are further fragmented between the Karachi Metropolitan Corporation (KMC) and provincial authorities, making coordinated urban development all the more difficult.
The problem, however, extends far beyond the quantum of development spending. While several new development schemes have been announced for Karachi, those still enduring the (now) five-year-long nightmare of construction along University Road know all too well that such projects bring far greater disruption than promise. Competing political interests, overlapping institutional mandates, and the persistent power struggle between provincial and local authorities undermine the effective and timely implementation of development projects.
Karachi is not simply a poorly developed city; it is an economically indispensable one whose governance arrangements systematically undermine its capacity to convert economic activity into better urban outcomes. The political economy underpinning the disparity between the two cities is hardly difficult to discern. Unlike Islamabad, where the Capital Development Authority provides a relatively centralised structure for urban planning and development, Karachi is governed through a maze of overlapping jurisdictions, with municipal authorities, cantonment boards, development authorities, and provincial departments each vying for greater control. Competing interests and distorted mandates make it difficult to establish who is ultimately responsible for the city’s development, leaving its residents to bear the cost of institutional dysfunction. Moreover, a weak municipal revenue base and limited capacity for own-source revenue mobilisation leave local governments heavily dependent on provincial transfers, further entrenching their fiscal dependence and weakening their capacity to deliver urban services.
It is deeply disheartening to see a city once synonymous with opportunity, enterprise, and the promise of a better life increasingly become a symbol of neglect, deprivation, and urban decay. Karachi needs more than sporadic development schemes and infrastructure projects. It needs empowered local governments, clearly defined institutional responsibilities, and predictable fiscal transfers that allow its elected representatives to plan and deliver services in line with the city’s needs. For a city that contributes so much to the country’s economy, the least it deserves is a governance system capable of delivering the most basic urban amenities.
Karachi deserves better.
The writer is a development economist and policy consultant. She teaches economics at IBA, Karachi.

title: Smog diplomacy
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
EACH winter, Lahore and Delhi engage in a peculiar rivalry, trading places at the top of the world’s air-pollution rankings. On Friday, Delhi was declared the world’s most polluted major city while Lahore slipped to seventh.
For people breathing this air, the distinction offers little comfort. A change in the weather can improve a city’s ranking without removing the sources of pollution.
The smog that settles over northern India and Pakistan comes from vehicle exhaust, industrial emissions, dust and agricultural fires, compounded by winter conditions that trap pollutants near the ground. Much of this pollution is generated locally, and both governments have work to do at home.
In Pakistan’s Punjab, satellites detected 18,825 fires, most believed to involve crop-residue burning. Lahore exceeded national standards for fine particulate matter on all 40 days covered by a recent assessment. Punjab’s authorities report more inspections, penalties and closures targeting polluting industries and brick kilns. Enforcement is necessary, but its effects must outlast the smog season.
    
There is also a regional dimension that neither government can afford to ignore. Polluted air crosses the border regardless of the state of bilateral relations. That makes the forthcoming visit of Pakistan’s climate change minister to New Delhi especially pertinent.
He is due to attend an SCO gathering on civilisational dialogue. Air pollution is not the meeting’s purpose, but the visit offers a rare opportunity to broach practical cooperation with Indian officials. At a minimum, the two states could work towards jointly sharing air-quality measurements, forecasts, timely public health warnings and satellite information on crop fires. Their scientists could jointly examine how pollution travels across the border.
    
Such efforts need not await a broader diplomatic thaw. Nor should they provide either side with an excuse to blame its neighbour for pollution it has failed to control at home.
The SCO already provides a channel through which officials from both countries meet, despite strained relations. The minister should use that opening to make the case for sustained regular technical contact on smog. With millions enduring another winter of dangerous air, even a modest conversation would be useful.

title: LG malaise
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE repeated delays in local government elections in Islamabad expose the reluctance of the government to strengthen democracy at the grassroots. The latest suspension by the IHC has again thrown the electoral process into uncertainty. The immediate dispute concerns the legal basis for delimitation. An ordinance issued in 2026 changed the capital’s LG structure. However, the ordinance lapsed, reviving the original 2015 law. The ECP proceeded with elections under the old law, even though the latest delimitation had been conducted under the new arrangement. This legal inconsistency has now stalled the electoral exercise. The problem goes beyond the latest dispute. Islamabad has been without an elected local government since February 2021. The ECP has conducted several delimitation exercises and announced multiple election schedules, but legislative changes and legal challenges have repeatedly disrupted the process.
In a related development, the ECP has given the Prime Minister’s Office a fortnight to formally request elections in 42 cantonment boards. Their elected LGs completed their terms in April. But the centre has still not fulfilled the procedural requirements for fresh polls. These developments point to a deeper problem. Successive governments have shown little enthusiasm for devolving political and administrative authority to local representatives. LGs create independent centres of political power and accountability. Federal and provincial governments often appear more comfortable retaining control over local development funds and administrative decisions than allowing local bodies to decide their priorities. This reluctance carries a direct cost for citizens. LGs are best placed to identify neighbourhood needs and address problems that larger tiers of government often overlook. These problems cannot be resolved by distant government departments. They need elected representatives who remain answerable to residents. The importance of effective LGs becomes even greater during emergencies. Without functioning local institutions, even well-funded disaster responses often struggle to reach communities quickly.
The constitutional requirement under Article 140-A to establish elected LGs reflects the importance of the third tier. Yet political commitments to devolution rarely translate into sustained institutional arrangements. Local bodies are allowed to function for limited periods before their terms expire, elections are delayed and administrative control returns to unelected officials. Electoral schedules should not remain hostage to indecision or repeated legislative changes. Residents deserve functioning local bodies that can address their everyday problems and respond when crises strike. Devolution must become a continuing democratic commitment rather than an arrangement governments honour only when convenient.
Published in Dawn, November 16th, 2026

title: Middle power aspirations
author: none@none.com (Khurram Abbas)
content:
AS the global order shifts away from unipolarity toward fragmented multipolarity, middle powers have gained unprecedented strategic weight. In a fragmented multipolar world, middle powers serve as indispensable diplomatic bridges and economic shock absorbers that keep the international system functioning despite great-power paralysis.
Middle powers lack hegemonic ambitions, and retain the credibility to mediate active conflicts, build agile issue-specific coalitions, and maintain open trade and supply-chain corridors across rival blocs. Ultimately, these middle powers are preventing total global bifurcation of the international system between Washington and Beijing by stabilising their immediate regions and upholding international rules.
However, scholars and policymakers rarely agree on a single checklist for middle power status, largely because different states exert influence through different mechanisms. Some, such as South Korea or Australia, earn the label through thriving, high-tech economies and global trade integration. Others, like Norway or Qatar, leverage niche diplomacy and active mediation to punch above their geographic weight. Still others, such as Türkiye and Pakistan, rely primarily on formidable military capabilities and regional security projection.
Scholars generally evaluate middle power status across three core pillars including military capability, diplomatic outreach, and comprehensive national strength. National strength is largely defined by sustainable economic vitality and technological adaptation.
    
Over the past two years, Pakistan has demonstrated a resurgence in the first two arenas, vaulting itself back into global strategic relevance. Yet, because its third and most foundational pillar remains weak, Pakistan’s recognition as an emerging middle power rests on a fragile foundation that cannot endure without a decisive domestic economic pivot.
A credible middle power must possess the military capacity to defend its sovereignty and project stabilising influence across its neighbourhood. Between 2025 and 2026, Pakistan highlighted its hard-power credentials through both high-intensity deterrence and institutionalised defence partnerships.
History shows that hard power and ingenious statecraft cannot substitute for domestic economic strength.
During the brief but severe four-day conflict with India in May 2025, South Asia witnessed its first multi-domain confrontation integrating aerial clashes, drone swarms, and precision missile exchanges. Pakistan’s military response, culminating in Operation Bunyanum Marsoos, demonstrated modern warfare capabilities and aerial superiority. Pakistan’s swift military response compelled a rapid White House-facilitated ceasefire on May 10. By denying a larger neighbour unilateral escalation dominance, Islamabad reinforced its conventional and strategic deterrence.
Since May 2025, Pakistan translated its battlefield credibility into a web of security pacts across the Middle East and the Muslim world.
In September 2025, Islamabad and Riyadh signed the Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement, and in August 2026, Pakistan joined Saudi Arabia and Türkiye to sign the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement. These pacts not only created a formal collective deterrence network but also enhanced Islamabad’s strategic utility in the Gulf. The Badr agreement with Türkiye, Qatar, and Indonesia, has further strengthened Pakistan’s position as a net security provider of Arab Gulf states.
Beyond military muscle, middle powers distinguish themselves through niche diplomacy. Following the outbreak of direct US-Israeli military hostilities against Iran in early 2026, traditional Gulf mediators found their channels strained. Adopting a posture of active neutrality, Islamabad stepped in.
In March 2026, the US accepted Pakistan’s role as a primary conduit to Tehran, which led to the historic Islamabad peace talks in April 2026 and the subsequent June MoU that temporarily reopened the Strait of Hormuz. Even as the truce faced repeated strain through late 2026, the civil and military leadership of Pakistan continued shuttling proposals between Washington, Tehran, and European capitals. The decision to join Trump’s Gaza peace plan as a founding member also proved Islamabad could exercise diplomatic power beyond its immediate borders.
However, despite these military and diplomatic milestones, history demonstrates that hard power and ingenious statecraft cannot substitute for domestic economic strength. In this third pillar, Pakistan exhibits severe structural deficits that undermine its middle power aspirations.
    
Macroeconomic indicators showed surface stabilisation in FY2025-26 with inflation remaining between 7-9 per cent and GDP growth edging up to 3.7pc. However, the underlying growth model remains weak. For instance, investment hovers near 15pc of GDP, far below the 20-plus per cent threshold required to sustain the 6pc growth rates needed to absorb a booming youth population. Deindustrialisation and high energy costs continue to stifle export competitiveness. Foreign investors are largely concerned with the security situation in Balochistan and KP. Unrest in AJK has further marred prospects of foreign direct investment.
The privatisation process is critically slow, while political consensus is absent over reforms for new provinces. With a low tax-to-GDP ratio and heavy external debt servicing, state solvency still relies heavily on remittances, multilateral bailouts, bilateral rollovers (such as a $3 billion Saudi cash deposit in April 2026) rather than productive capital formation.
Hence, Pakistan today represents a textbook case of an asymmetric emerging middle power. Its disciplined military and seasoned diplomatic corps have successfully leveraged regional crises to earn Islamabad a seat at high-stakes global tables. However, geopolitical leverage built on security crises and external rent is inherently transactional. When regional wars subside or great-power priorities shift, Islamabad — lacking economic autonomy and technological innovation — will risk losing its strategic relevance.
Therefore, to cement its status as a genuine middle power, Pakistan must execute an urgent domestic pivot. This requires dismantling elite economic capture, broadening the tax base, overhauling education to build a tech-literate workforce, and enhancing an export-driven industrial base. Until Islamabad matches its battlefield deterrence and diplomatic agility with sustainable economic sovereignty, its middle power status will remain an aspiration suspended over a precarious fault line.
The writer is a strategic analyst of international security. The views expressed are his own.

title: Muddled hierarchy
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE Federal Constitutional Court marked its first anniversary on Friday with a commemorative stamp. Speaking on the occasion, its chief justice remarked on how fleeting the year had been. Litigants, lawyers and the judges of the Supreme Court might have described it differently. A year after the 27th Amendment rewrote the structure of the country’s judiciary, one of the most basic questions raised by the new order remains unanswered: which court, the FCC or the SC, has the final word? This was, perhaps, bound to happen. Critics had foreseen problems in the short and hurried route the government took from the 26th to the 27th Amendment.
In October 2024, the 26th Amendment carved constitutional benches out of the SC, with their members chosen by a reconstituted Judicial Commission in which judges no longer held a majority. Critics warned then that the independence of the judiciary was at stake. Barely a year later, and in evident haste, the 27th Amendment turned those benches into an entirely separate court. Two of the SC’s senior-most judges resigned in protest the day it became law. Thousands of cases were soon transferred to the FCC, and the SC was stripped of its constitutional jurisdiction. What has followed has seemed less a division of labour than a contest for primacy. Last December, the FCC held that its rulings bind all courts, including the SC, but that the latter’s do not bind the FCC. In May, Chief Justice Yahya Afridi pushed back, ruling that the two are coordinate courts, neither an appellate forum over the other. Last month, the FCC rebuked an SC bench for revisiting a matter the FCC considered settled, raising concerns over judicial discipline. The sparring shows no sign of stopping.
The text of the amendment arguably favours the FCC, while the SC relies on the overall constitutional scheme to assert its position. That both positions can be argued is precisely the problem. Two hasty amendments have created an ambiguity that leaves the two courts defining their relationship through pointed observations in their judgments. The costs are borne by litigants, whose cases risk being shuttled between forums. The FCC, meanwhile, has worked with seven judges against a sanctioned strength of 13. And its order barring the Peshawar High Court from hearing petitions on emergency and governor’s rule in KP has pushed citizens away from a court closer to home. Since parliament created this ambiguity, it must now resolve it. The jurisdiction of the two courts and a mechanism for settling disputes between them should be spelt out in law, not left to judges to fight over. Lastly, the judiciary’s structure is not its only problem. As long as its independence remains in doubt, it will struggle to win public confidence.
Published in Dawn, November 15th, 2026

title: Growing crisis
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
AN emergency can be judged by the speed with which it draws an effective response. The National Population Council’s executive committee has declared rapid population growth a national emergency. But Pakistan has been warned about this crisis for decades, with little to show for it. People still struggle to obtain reproductive healthcare, clinics run short of contraceptives, and millions of couples lack the information and services needed to plan families. The 2023 census recorded an annual population growth rate of 2.55pc, placing further pressure on schools, hospitals, housing, jobs and water supplies. The state cannot keep announcing plans while failing to provide basic services. One key decision taken at the meeting was to improve the tracking of contraceptive supplies. But collecting data is only the first step. Provinces must ensure that clinics are adequately equipped, healthcare workers are trained and family planning services reach remote and neglected communities. Religious scholars can also help address misconceptions about birth spacing, particularly by explaining its benefits for mothers and children.
Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal has raised another important issue: the National Finance Commission formula, which gives population an 82pc weight in the distribution of provincial resources. His concern that the formula may reward population growth deserves attention. However, simply giving provinces more money for reducing birth rates could create fresh problems. Provinces with larger, poorer populations already face greater demands for schools, hospitals and other services. Cutting their share would only make these problems worse. Instead, the government should consider rewarding provinces that improve access to family planning, girls’ education and maternal healthcare, while ensuring that funding reflects their actual needs. Above all, the authorities must recognise that population planning is about helping people make informed choices, not merely bringing down numbers. Calling population growth a national emergency is easy. Ensuring that the response reaches the people who need it is the real challenge.

title: Judges must speak
author: none@none.com (Justice (retd) Syed Mansoor Ali Shah)
content:
A JUDGMENT is a public document, written in the name of the Constitution and delivered in open court. The people may read it, praise it and criticise it, and the academy, bar, press and civil society should do so freely. Criticism is not the enemy of judicial authority; it is its source. A judiciary whose judgments are never read critically will never grow.
One voice is largely missing from that conversation: the judge who wrote the judgment. In Pakistan, judges mostly retire into silence. That must change. Retired judges must come out among the people, above all into the law schools, and explain their reasoning, or say, with hindsight: “I think I got that one wrong.” Such candour teaches the profession and builds public trust and confidence in the institution. A sitting judge who knows retirement means facing the public will brush nothing under the carpet.
A judgment open to criticism falls into one of three kinds. The first plainly violates the Constitution and the law. The second was legally permissible when given, but its consequences proved damaging. The third is the judgment in which the judge was complicit, bending the law to reach an outcome decided elsewhere.
To assess one, read it whole and in context: the moment, the circumstances, the law as it then stood. Then ask whether it was permissible, plainly wrong, or the judge simply listening to power.
Let me test three of my own.
In Pakistan, judges mostly retire into silence. That must change.
In the 2023 case on Punjab and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa elections, Justice Jamal Khan Mandokhail and I wanted the high courts to decide first: Lahore had already ordered elections, with appeals pending, and Peshawar was seized of the petitions. Law and practice both counselled that restraint. We read the outcome as four to three, because two colleagues who had already voted to dismiss could not, in our view, be dropped from the count; Justice Athar Minallah, one of them, recorded as much.
    
In hindsight, the mistake, I believe, was the chief justice’s hurried leap in; hearing the matter in appeal, the court could have spoken with one voice. Had we set the count aside and presented a united court, whether that would have produced elections is anyone’s guess. Later, the chief justice’s own bench rejected the four-three objection and fixed May 14 for Punjab polls, yet could not enforce it. The date passed, contempt was never pursued, and the court fell silent.
The larger lesson is that a court must stand united, and the chief justice’s strength is the real spine that holds it together. The Supreme Court as it stands today shows how much rests on that spine.
In the Justice Qazi Faez Isa case, the court unanimously quashed the reference, the majority for malice in law; I held it malicious in fact as well. The majority directed the FBR to examine the family’s properties and report to the council; three of us held that no direction was needed, the FBR being free to act under the tax law. On review, that view prevailed.
No one is above the law, and no one below its protection: a judge’s spouse answers under the tax law, a judge under the Code of Conduct, only in accordance with law. I am often asked whether we saved the wrong man. We saved due process and the independence of the judiciary, and in doing so we saved a man. What people thought of him later was not our concern then. A judgment is not a character certificate.
In the Practice and Procedure case, I believed, and still believe, that the court had to become collegial rather than be run by one man. Opening the door was not itself the mistake; so long as the court stood united, no one could have walked through it. What we failed to see was that the court was weak within, and weakness inside invites those outside. And it did: a 2024 ordinance gave the chief justice’s nominee a seat on the bench-forming committee. Had earlier chief justices brought in the collegial model through the full court, that door need never have opened from outside. This is a lesson, not an accusation.
Each choice was made in good faith, within the law. In hindsight, wiser choices may have been available, but choosing in the moment is the judicial function, and there the judge must be trusted. Unless a judge was complicit, there is nothing to apologise for, only lessons to share.
    
What must worry us most is complicity. It is not an error of judgment but a surrender of it, and it has hollowed out our courts. A judgment bent to power may be overruled, but the betrayal stays on the record. Error is part of judging. Capitulation is not. And complicity has a way of showing its face, in the promotions, benefits and advantages that later reward it. Today, that trail must be made visible.
A word to the critics. Those quick to call out judicial error must be as open-hearted in acknowledging courage. Dissent, refusal of oath and resignation are the building blocks of an independent judiciary. Ask what a judge gained by resigning when a simple yes would have secured everything. Nothing, except the honour of the institution. Criticism that records every failure and never that courage leaves the next generation no one to look up to.
So let the conversation begin, and let it be honest. Let judges speak: give the context of their decisions, own their errors without fear and explain their choices without apology. And let complicity be named for what it is.
Judicial independence has never been absolute. Sadly, there has always been a chink in the armour, a door left ajar, and someone willing to push it open. No single judgment or judge will close that door. But an honest and open conversation, carried from one generation to the next, can. That will be the real victory: not a court that never errs, but a court with no door through which power can enter.
The writer is a professor of practice at SAHSOL, Lums, and currently a distinguished visiting fellow at Yale University.
Published in Dawn, November 15th, 2026

title: China’s modernisation models
author: none@none.com (Syed Sardar Ali)
content:
PAKISTAN was the first Muslim country to recognise the People’s Republic of China (PRC), with the two countries establishing diplomatic ties on May 21, 1951. During the past 75 years, the relationship has blossomed into an “all-wea­ther strategic cooperative partnership.” During the 1950s and 1960s, despite being a member of Western security alliances, Pakistan helped Beij­ing break out of its international isolation. Islam­abad’s diplomatic mediation in the early 1970s helped in the historic rapprochement between China and the United States. Reciprocally, China has supported Pakistan economically, militarily, and diplomatically, providing unwavering support for its national sovereignty, territorial integrity, and socioeconomic stability.
The PRC was established as a single-party ideological state in the Marxist-Leninist tradition. Under the British legacy, Pakistan established a federal state and Westminster-style parliamentary democracy. These governance structures have led to divergence in the modernisation trajectories of the two countries, despite the adoption of similar reform policies.
Both China and Pakistan have attempted to resolve the issue of inequitable distribution of agricultural land. The Communist Party of China (CPC) solved the problem by distributing land titles to 300 million peasants using radical measures. Despite possessing less than 10 per cent of the world’s arable land, China produces about 25pc of global grain output. In Pakistan, landlords undermined all attempts at land reforms by falsifying records. Currently, 67pc rural households in Pakistan own no land. Despite having the world’s largest contiguous canal system, Pakistan is ranked 106 out of 123 countries in the Global Hunger Index.
The ideal of women’s emancipation has been pursued by both China and Pakistan. Starting with the Marriage Law of 1950, China has passed nearly 100 laws and regulations, including the landmark Law on the Protection of Rights and Interests of Women 1992. Today China, at 65pc, is ahead of the global average in female labour for­ce participation. Traditionally, family life in Pak­­istan has been ruled by feudal and tribal cust­o­­ms, colonial-era personal laws, and religious precepts. Pakistan promulgated the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961 but conditions in rural areas remained unchanged. In the Global Gender Gap Index of the World Economic Forum, Pakis­t­­an ranks at the very bottom: 148 out of 148 countries.
In China, modernisation emerged as one of the central purposes of the state.
Soviet-style five-year plans have been used by both China and Pakistan. Since 1953, China has successfully completed 15 five-year plans. In the process it has been transformed from a subsistence agricultural economy into the largest manufacturing power, the biggest exporter, and the only country in history to achieve a trade surplus of one trillion dollars. Pakistan has implemented eight five-year plans but only the second plan (1960-65) succeeded in achieving its targets. Pakistan discontinued the practice in 1998. Slow growth in the last two decades has pushed Pakistan below its South Asian neighbours in per capita GDP. The country runs an annual trade deficit of around $30 billion and Pakistan has received more assistance packages from the International Monetary Fund than any other country.
Similar modernisation measures producing dissimilar outcomes is the result of differences in political ideology, structure of the state, and form of government of China and Pakistan.
From the British, Pakistan inherited the tradition of liberalism where the state exists primarily to protect individual rights and private property. It is not an instrument to achieve national goals. Socialism distinguishes between different modes of production and the state is an agent of progress. In China, modernisation emerged as one of the central purposes of the state and the supreme responsibility of the party. Political debates in Pakistan remain confined to changes of government. In Pakistan, modernisation never became the topic of political debate and state resources have never been marshalled to achieve it.
In China, the CPC solved the problem of lack of state institutions by building party network. Fusion of the party and the state meant that the party’s directives and policies were seamlessly translated into state legislation and administrative action. The party-state model has proved to be the perfect strategy for building modern bureaucracy. Pakistan inherited the colonial-era civil service but nepotism and patronage gradually eroded its essence of impersonality, specialisation, and merit. With every political government the capacity of the state declined, rendering it incapable of maintaining security, collecting taxes, and enforcing policies.
Pakistan adopted multiparty adult franchise democracy but the society had no tradition of resolution of differences through rational discourse, no common civic public good, and no equality. Inevitably, Pakistan’s democracy morphed into demagoguery and populism. The communists enshrined in the Chinese constitution the CPC’s leadership as a foundational pillar of the Chinese state. This allows the ruling party to focus on governance. While Pakistan’s political institutions have pushed the country ever deeper into crises, the combination of progressive ideology, appropriate state model, and correct governance system has allowed China to focus on the grand project of national rejuvenation.
For developing countries, the universal lesson is that modernisation is not possible without an effective state but not all state types are equal in their capacity. The Westphalian state model and universal-franchise democracy, when adopted by non-Western societies, do not necessarily result in a functional state and a stable government. To be effective, a state and its governance system must align with local conditions and be in harmony with society’s stage of evolution. Without an effective state machinery, even the most elaborate modernisation plans can neither foster sustainable development nor secure a happy and prosperous life for the people.
The writer has a background in public administration. He has worked with international financial institutions, including the World Bank.
Published in Dawn, November 14th, 2026

title: Derailed by design
author: none@none.com (Naeem Sadiq)
content:
PAKISTAN Railways has become synonymous with the image of a decaying organisation: accident-prone, loss-making and inefficient. Not many are willing to admit that mismanagement, unsteady wagons, rickety tracks and 18th-century mindset have reduced the Railways to a near-death existence. Even when it reluctantly continues to chug, rattle and rumble, everyone knows that it is managed and operated in a way not much different from a lorry adda across the road. The only option left seems to lie in the old Dakota Indian tribal wisdom: “When you discover that you are riding a dead horse, the best strategy is to dismount.”
Pakistan Railways has simply run out of steam. A meltdown was only natural. Managerially, technically and financially bankrupt, it finds it impossible to transport passengers and goods safely and efficiently. It is headed by a bureaucrat and a politician. While declaring a railway emergency, the only actions the minister in charge could think of were punishments received by schoolchildren. Come to work on Sundays, no leave for three months, send daily reports (homework) to the ministry and use trains for travelling on duty.
Even a novice would immediately figure out the pointlessness of these measures. A better informed and competent management would have suggested identifying root causes, taking actions to prevent their recurrence and verifying them for their effectiveness.
Imagine a railway in the year 2026 that cannot use even a basic email system for its routine internal and external communication (a disease proudly shared by the entire government of Pakistan.) Reportedly, an experimental email was recently sent to 40 senior officials of the Railways. Thirty-nine never responded, while one was responded to by a clerk saying that a reply was not possible due to the absence of the boss.
Pakistan Railways needs non-political & professional management.
Compare the sense of responsibility and ethics that differentiate Pakistan Railways from the rest of the world. Following the train derailment at Hatfield, UK on Oct 17, 2000, which killed four passengers, the Railtrack CEO Gerald Corbett took less than 24 hours to tender his resignation. Mohsen Aghaie, the head of the Iranian Railways was quick to resign after a train collision that killed 44 people in Iran in November 2016, describing his departure as a matter of social responsibility and sympathy for the survivors.
Pakistan Railways, on the other hand, met with 448 railway disasters between 2021 and 2025, leaving 169 dead and over 400 injured or crippled for life. Not a single Railways chairman even remotely contemplated a resignation. There is no record of any official above grade 19 ever having been held accountable. No wonder the lack of accountability has helped the Railways perfect the art of digging progressively deeper pits and incurring bigger losses each year. It incurred a financial loss of Rs47.49 billion in 2022, Rs48.2bn in 2023, Rs51.38bn in 2024 and Rs61.19bn in 2025. What crime have the people of Pakistan committed to carry such loss-making and life-extracting burden on their shoulders?
Track-related derailments, unmanned crossings and train collisions are the three most cited reasons for the repeated railway accidents. Pakistan Railways management has been negligent of not addressing these issues. A quick root cause analysis and effective corrective actions could have fixed these issues for good. Not equipped to either think or act on modern professional lines, it has finally come to an expected dead end.
Can a clueless bureaucratic structure that allows hu­­man waste to fall directly on railway tracks, from stationary and moving tra­ins, be entrus­t­­ed to underta­ke the task of running a Railways system?
Pakistan Ra-ilways needs to replace its current setup with a completely non-political, non-bureaucratic and professional management. It needs a world-class occupational health and safety system. It needs a proactive hazard identification and risk assessment programme to fix its fragile tracks, its 1,416 unmanned crossings, and its archaic communication system.
For all this, the Railways does not need billions of dollars. It needs billions of neurons. Every developed country’s railway has a system called Occupational Health and Safety Management System based on national or international standards such as ISO 45001.
Pakistan Railways appears to have no clue of any such system. Being an occupational health and safety engineer, may I humbly offer to spend two months (as an entirely pro bono activity) to help Pakistan Railways set up such a world-class safety management system.
The writer is an industrial engineer and a volunteer social activist.

title: Pakistan’s polio paradox
author: none@none.com (Fayyaz Ahmad Khan)
content:
PAKISTAN’S latest polio case, a seven-month-old boy in Khyber district reported on Nov 6, is the ninth of 2026 and the seventh in Khyber Pakh­tun­khwa. It is another reminder of how elusive eradication has proved. After three decades of campa­i­gns, billions of dollars of international support, a field force of more than 400,000 workers, and the creation of one of the largest polio programmes in the world, the country has still not eliminated a pre­­ventable disease. Pakistan has not turned its abi­­lity to run campaigns into a system of public health protection that families trust, and that failure, which lies behind much of the refusal, is why the virus survives.
The obstacles usually cited are real: insecurity, population movement, and difficult terrain keep teams from some children, while refusals, misinformation, and religious misconceptions keep others from being vaccinated. They do not account for the survival of the virus in communities that vaccination teams reach campaign after campaign and where families still turn the teams away. The reason lies beyond the vaccine, in the relationship between the state, its health institutions, and the communities they serve, and in whether those communities trust them.
Political scientist Bo Rothstein has argued that trust in government depends on the quality and im­­partiality of public institutions: people trust ins­­titutions they experience as fair and reliable. Com­munication alone does not build trust, and a nati­onal health priority cannot command it. It grows out of people’s everyday experience of the state.
The polio programme mobilises on a scale few public institutions in Pakistan can match. It deploys hundreds of thousands of vaccinators, maps households, monitors coverage, and returns repeatedly for the children who were missed. That capacity has saved many thousands of children from paralysis and remains essential to eradication. Beside that achievement stands the failure: the state’s ability to reach almost every household with polio drops has not become a working system of routine immunisation and basic healthcare.
For many families, particularly in underserved parts of the country, the polio team may be one of the few regular points of contact with the state. A vaccinator arrives at the doorstep, sometimes several times a year, to administer polio drops. The same household may have no functioning health facility within reach, no routine childhood vaccines, no maternal care, and no clean drinking water. The state is visible when it wants to vaccinate a child, and often invisible when that child or family needs anything else.
Pakistan’s polio programme has acknowledged that communities are using demand-based boycotts as a bargaining chip to draw attention to their problems.
The contrast is sharpest in southern KP, where communities have boycotted polio campaigns to press the government on demands that have gone unanswered for years. Misinformation and religious opposition explain few of these boycotts.
The British Medical Journal reported in December 2023 that tribal jirgas in southern KP had declared 677 boycotts during the year, with demands that ran from electricity, roads, and livelihoods to ref­u­­se collection. Pakistan’s own polio programme ack­nowledged that communities were using dem­and-based boycotts as a bargaining chip to draw attention to their problems. When a vaccination rou­­nd is the only occasion on which citizens can obtain ba­­sic services, the fault lies in the system of government as a whole. In some places a boycott is one of the few acts to which the government is compelled to respond, and communities have learnt as much.
The frontline has weaknesses of its own. Too few female vaccinators and frequent changes of team members, with thin training for all of them, spoil the encounter at the door. Vaccinators do not always explain convincingly why a child needs repeated doses, least of all to parents who believe that earlier campaigns should have been enough, and programmes make too little use of trusted local figures who understand the concerns of families. Even a better trained and more persuasive team, though, cannot make up for the absence of reliable public services.
Repeated visits can also do harm when families experience them as an imposition. For families who see little improvement in their lives, each arrival of a polio team can confirm that the state cares about one disease and one campaign, and little about the wellbeing of their children.
The response is to make vaccination part of a broader and more consistent public health presen­­ce, by strengthening routine immunisation and pri­­mary healthcare. The outreach capacity the pol­io programme has built should find the children rou­­tine immunisation has missed and connect their families with regular health services. That takes trained health workers, reliable vaccine supplies, accessible facilities, and continuity of care, well beyond the occasional catch-up activities atta­ched to polio campaigns, so that immunisation beco­mes a regular function of the district health system.
Behind this is the institutional separation between the polio programme and the wider health system. For years the National and Provincial Emergency Operations Centres have run as a well-funded parallel structure, answerable in large part to international donors, which mobilises large resources for campaign days while the provincial health departments beside them remain short of funds and bound by procedure. The dedicated funding, staffing, surveillance, and management arrangements that let the polio programme operate at scale belong inside the permanent health infrastructure of the provinces.
Communities also need channels for their wider concerns, through local administration and elected representatives, and those channels have to work independently of vaccination campaigns. Otherwise the government teaches communities that withholding children from vaccination is an effective way to secure electricity, water, or roads.
The responsibility rests with the Ministry of National Health Services, Regulations and Coordination, with the provincial governments, above all in KP, and with international donors, who should measure success by the strength of district health services as well as by the number of children reached in each round. Eradication depends on the campaigns, with better trained and more representative teams, and on what the campaigns cannot supply: a health system that protects children between rounds.
When a vaccination team arrives at a door, the family should see it as part of a state that also protects their children and listens to them. Until that is so, Pakistan may go on running polio campaigns, and the conditions that make eradication so difficult will stay as they are.
The writer is a strategic communication and public health professional, with experience across Asia, Africa and the Middle East.
